question: Why do critical notifications (OTP, security alerts) need a separate queue rather than a shared one with priority?

options.text: In a shared queue, millions of promotional emails can block OTP processing. Separate queues provide physical isolation: critical workers don't compete with low-priority for resources
options.explanation: Physical isolation (separate queue + dedicated workers) guarantees that 10 million promotional messages won't delay an SMS authorization code. This is called priority inversion prevention — critical messages are processed independently of background task volume

options.text: Separate queues are faster because Redis works more efficiently with short lists
options.explanation: Redis performance doesn't significantly depend on list length for LPUSH/LPOP operations. The reason is resource isolation: critical queues have dedicated workers that don't compete with mass mailings for CPU and network

options.text: Kafka doesn't support priorities within a single topic
options.explanation: While Kafka indeed has no built-in priorities, this is merely a technical implementation detail. The main reason is architectural: physical isolation guarantees that mass mailings won't affect the delivery time of critical messages

options.text: This is only needed for compliance — regulators require channel separation
options.explanation: Compliance may require logging and auditing, but queue separation is an architectural decision to ensure SLA on critical notification delivery time, not a regulatory requirement

question: Apple Push Notification Service (APNs) returns a Feedback Service with a list of invalid device tokens. What happens if you ignore this feedback?

options.text: Apple will start throttling (rate limiting) your push notifications, and may eventually block your certificate
options.explanation: APNs tracks how many messages you send to invalid tokens. A high percentage of invalid sends → Apple reduces your delivery speed (throttling). With systematic ignoring — certificate blocking. Similar to email: high bounce rate → landing in spam

options.text: Nothing — APNs silently drops messages to invalid tokens without consequences
options.explanation: APNs doesn't stay silent — it tracks invalid sends. Continuing to send to invalid tokens wastes resources and risks throttling from Apple. The Feedback Service exists specifically so you can clean up invalid tokens

options.text: Push notifications will pile up in the APNs queue and will be delivered when the user turns on their device
options.explanation: An invalid token means the app was deleted or reinstalled — the device is no longer bound to that token. APNs doesn't accumulate messages for invalid tokens; it drops them immediately

options.text: APNs automatically removes invalid tokens from your database
options.explanation: APNs has no access to your database. It only provides a Feedback Service — an API from which you can retrieve the list of invalid tokens. Removing them from your DB is your responsibility

question: A service sends a notification but gets a timeout from the push provider. On retry — the user receives 2 identical pushes. How to prevent this?

options.text: Use an idempotency key: before sending, record the key in Redis; on retry, check — if the key exists, don't resend
options.explanation: An idempotency key (e.g., eventId + userId + channel) guarantees exactly-once semantics at the sending level. Even if the first request actually reached the provider (timeout doesn't mean failure), the retry will be blocked. Redis SET with TTL = 24h is sufficient for deduplication

options.text: Set a longer timeout (30 seconds) to never get a timeout
options.explanation: Increasing the timeout doesn't solve the problem — timeouts will still occur during network failures. Moreover, a 30-second timeout for critical OTP notifications is unacceptable. The correct approach is idempotency, not avoiding errors

options.text: Don't retry on timeout — if there's no response, it means it was delivered
options.explanation: A timeout can mean either successful delivery (response was lost) or complete failure (provider server is down). Refusing to retry for critical notifications (OTP code) is unacceptable — the user won't receive the authorization code. Retry with deduplication is needed

options.text: Ask the push provider whether the message was delivered, and only then decide on retry
options.explanation: APNs and FCM don't provide a synchronous API to 'check if a specific message was delivered'. Delivery receipts come asynchronously via webhook and may not arrive at all. The only reliable approach is an idempotency key on the sender's side

question: When designing a Notification System, which pipeline stages must be completed BEFORE enqueuing for delivery?

options.explanation: Deduplication before the queue prevents duplicates from entering. If you deduplicate after the queue, producer retries will put duplicates into the queue, and each will be processed by a separate worker

options.text: User preference check (channels, quiet hours, unsubscribes)
options.explanation: Filtering by preferences before the queue saves resources: why enqueue a push if the user disabled push notifications? This removes up to 30–50% of unnecessary messages from the queue

Templates are rendered before the queue so that the queue contains a finished message. Otherwise, workers would need to access the DB for templates and data — additional network calls in the delivery hot path
Delivery status comes AFTER sending, not before enqueuing. This is an asynchronous process: webhooks from SendGrid/Twilio/APNs update the status after the worker has sent the message
